subject: Business
title: Moore's Law and Exponential Progress
description: A quick win: understand Moore's Law and Exponential Progress.

hook.text: Your smartphone has more computing power than all of NASA had during the 1969 moon landing.

buildup.text: Moore's Law: the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years, making computers exponentially faster.

discovery.text: This exponential curve drove the price of computing down from $1 trillion per gigaflop in 1961 to $0.03 today.

twist.text: Humans think linearly but technology grows exponentially. We consistently underestimate what's possible in 10 years.

climax.text: Moore's Law enabled smartphones, AI, cloud computing, and self-driving cars — each impossible without cheap, fast chips.

punchline.text: The most dangerous prediction: 'That'll never be fast enough.'

quiz.question: What does Moore's Law describe?
options: Transistor count on chips doubles roughly every two years

details.summary: Moore's Law observed that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles approximately every two years, making computing exponentially cheaper and more powerful. This exponential trend has held for over 50 years, driving virtually every digital technology advancement in modern history.
details.whyItMatters: Moore's Law explains why a smartphone now has more computing power than NASA had for the moon landing. Understanding exponential technological progress helps anticipate future possibilities that linear thinking dramatically underestimates.
takeaways: Transistor density on chips doubles roughly every two years since the 1960s
Exponential progress compounds into million-fold improvements over decades
Human brains think linearly, making exponential trends counterintuitive

faq.question: Is Moore's Law still valid in the 2020s?
faq.answer: Traditional transistor scaling is slowing due to physical limits at atomic scales. However, innovation continues through new architectures, chiplet designs, 3D stacking, and specialized processors. The spirit of exponential improvement continues even if the specific transistor metric is changing.

faq.question: Why does exponential progress feel sudden even though it is gradual?
faq.answer: Exponential curves start slowly and appear flat for a long time. Doubling from one million to two million is barely noticeable. But doubling from one billion to two billion is dramatic. The same rate of progress produces increasingly visible results as the base grows larger.
